meta.subtitle: Every segment grew and capital return runs at $8 billion a quarter; the debate is how much of the fee income is cyclical

analystSentiment.commentary:
Bank of America's second quarter of 2026 was the quarter the franchise had been building toward. Revenue, net of interest expense, rose {+ +15% +} year over year to $31.6 billion, net income rose to $9.1 billion, diluted EPS rose {+ +34% +} to $1.21, and the efficiency ratio improved to 59% on 6.6% of operating leverage. Return on average tangible common shareholders' equity reached 17.0%, the CET1 ratio held at 11.2% above its 10% minimum, and the quarter's capital return was followed by a dividend increase to $0.32 declared July 23, 2026.

Two facts about the pack shape how we read the numbers. The vendor's income model is not bank-shaped, and the financials section explains the basis difference once; we work from the release and the 10-Q, where revenue is net of interest expense. And the headline capture returned the bank's own research notes on other companies rather than news about the bank, so this report carries no post-quarter news flow.

We rate the shares BUY. At 12.8x NTM earnings the shares trade below their 13.5x trailing multiple and a little above the ~11.3x the current price implies on FY27E, for a bank earning that return on tangible equity, whose tangible book value per share rose 7% over the year to $29.37 and whose consensus EPS grows from $4.64 in FY26E to $5.26 in FY27E. The counter-case is the one the risk section argues: the quarter's fee revenue sits at a cyclical high, and a lower-rate path works against net interest income just as the deposit franchise's advantage is being priced. Our probability-weighted value lands above the current price by about the margin consensus already assumes, and the target range is $62–$72.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Bank of America Corporation is a Delaware bank holding company and financial holding company headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, operating mainly through the Bank of America, N.A. charter. At June 30, 2026 it had $3.5 trillion in assets, approximately 211,000 employees and operations across the U.S. and more than 35 countries. It serves more than 69 million consumer and small business clients through approximately 3,500 retail financial centers, approximately 15,000 ATMs and digital platforms with approximately 50 million active users, and its wealth businesses hold client balances of approximately $4.9 trillion.

The 10-Q reports four business segments: Consumer Banking, Global Wealth & Investment Management (GWIM), Global Banking and Global Markets, with remaining operations in All Other. The vendor's FY25 mix, which the segment chart follows, puts Consumer Banking at 37.4% ($43.7B), Global Wealth and Investment Management at 21.3% ($24.9B), Global Banking at 20.6% ($24.1B) and Global Markets at 20.6% ($24.1B) of segment revenue. The vendor's geographic split lists a Non-US total of 12.0% alongside its regional components, so the chart double counts outside the U.S.; the usable figure is the United States at 76.0%.

What the second quarter of 2026 shows is the shape of the earnings: revenue, net of interest expense, split almost evenly between net interest income of $15,997 million and noninterest income of $15,561 million, with average deposits of $2.02 trillion funding average loans and leases of $1.22 trillion. A bank earning half its revenue from fees and funded mostly by deposits rather than borrowings is a different animal from a spread lender, and that is why the vendor's industrial template, which the financials section translates, does not fit it.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body:
Bank of America earns its return three ways, and all three improved in the second quarter of 2026. Net interest income rose {+ +9% +} to $16.0 billion as fixed-rate assets repriced and higher-cost funding was repaid, noninterest income rose {+ +22% +} on wealth fees, investment banking and trading, and noninterest expense rose a slower 8% to $18.6 billion, which produced 6.6% of operating leverage and a 59% efficiency ratio. Provision for credit losses fell to $1.4 billion from $1.6 billion a year earlier, and net charge-offs were flat to the March quarter and down from $1.5 billion a year earlier.

The cyclical pieces, trading and investment banking, sit on top of a deposit and lending franchise compounding on its own: average deposits of $2.02 trillion grew for a twelfth consecutive quarter of sequential average growth, average loans of $1.22 trillion rose by $88 billion, and the CET1 ratio of 11.2% leaves room to keep returning capital while risk-weighted assets grow. At 12.8x NTM earnings, with tangible book value per share up 7% to $29.37 and a dividend just raised 14 percent, the shares are paid to compound, and we rate them BUY. The bear case is a rate cycle that compresses net interest income faster than fees and buybacks can offset, and a normalization in the fee lines.

catalysts: Full-year operating leverage guidance was raised mid-year, and 2027 will be measured against it; the growth section carries the figures.
The quarterly dividend of $0.32 declared July 23, 2026 is payable September 25, 2026, and the quarter's repurchases are the near-term support for the shares.
Net interest yield rose year over year as fixed-rate assets reprice, and management says the repricing is ongoing.
Commercial lending is leading loan growth, and management describes investment banking pipelines as strong.
AI-enabled productivity that management says is now embedded across operations and client-facing teams; it would show in the expense line, and it is not yet separable in the numbers.
risks: Rate cuts: the risk section carries the 10-K's mechanism and the offset management cites.
Fee revenue at a cyclical high: the two fee lines with the sharpest growth in the quarter are the ones a market downturn removes first.
Credit: provision and net charge-offs were flat quarter over quarter, but reservable criticized commercial exposures still stand near $22 billion.
Litigation and regulation: the 10-Q lists open matters from unemployment-benefit processing to Zelle fraud, alongside capital rules from stress buffers to the GSIB surcharge.
Governance: Say on Pay drew 73.6% support at the 2025 meeting and the Chair and CEO roles are combined; the management section carries the proxy detail.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The vendor's income table needs a translation before it can be read, and this is the one place the report makes it. Its revenue is gross of interest expense, so the FY21–FY25 series ($93.9B to $191.6B, with growth of +22.6%, +49.4% and +11.9% in FY22–FY24) mostly measures the rise in interest rates passing through gross interest income, and its gross margin (99.8% in FY21, 56.1% in FY25) is revenue net of interest expense as a share of that gross figure; neither is a franchise metric. The same applies to the quarter: the snapshot's Q2'26 revenue of $49.4B (+6%) is the vendor's gross figure, while the 10-Q and the release report revenue net of interest expense of $31.6 billion, up 15% from $27.4 billion a year earlier, and the report uses the latter throughout. Consensus FY26E revenue of ~$124B carries no basis note; our reading is that it sits on the bank's net basis, because the six months to June produced $61,830 million of revenue net of interest expense, a run-rate consistent with it, so the -35% shown next to FY25 is a change of basis rather than a forecast. Operating income is the cleaner series: $34.0B in FY21, a trough of $28.3B in FY23 as funding costs caught up with asset yields, and $37.7B in FY25, with net income of $30.5B and diluted EPS of $3.82.

On the bank's own basis the second quarter of 2026 reads as follows. Net interest income was $16.0 billion, up 9%, on a net interest yield that rose to 2.08 percent, and noninterest income was $15,561 million, up from $12,773 million. Noninterest expense of $18.6 billion rose 8%, split by the release equally between revenue-related expense and investment in people, brand and technology. Provision for credit losses was $1.4 billion, down from $1.6 billion, and pretax income rose to $11.6 billion from $8.7 billion. Net income was $9.1 billion, diluted EPS $1.21 from $0.90, and the efficiency ratio improved 359 bps to 59%. Return on average assets was 1.03%, return on average common equity 12.7% and return on average tangible common equity 17.0%; six-month diluted EPS was $2.31.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
A bank's balance sheet does not fit the vendor's template either. The table's FY25 total debt of $365.9B and net debt of $134.1B count only borrowings, not the deposits that fund most of the balance sheet, and its current ratio of 0.42 treats deposits as current liabilities over loans held as long-term assets; the trailing net debt to EBITDA of 15.4x and interest coverage of 0.6x fail for the same reason, since interest expense is a bank's cost of goods sold. What the 10-Q gives instead is the right frame. Total assets were $3,499,191 million at June 30, 2026, up $87.5 billion from year end on securities borrowed and customer receivables supporting Global Markets activity and on commercial loan growth, while debt securities ran off. Total deposits were $2,025,124 million compared with total loans and leases of $1,217,619 million, so the loan book is funded by deposits with room to spare, and the release puts average Global Liquidity Sources at $947 billion.

Capital is the constraint that matters. CET1 capital was $202 billion, up $1.9 billion from the March quarter, and the CET1 ratio was 11.2% on the standardized approach, which management says is well ahead of its 10% minimum; risk-weighted assets rose to $1.8 trillion on loan growth and markets activity. Total shareholders' equity fell $2.1 billion from December 31, 2025 to $301,094 million because repurchases, dividends, a preferred redemption and lower accumulated other comprehensive income outweighed net income, which is the arithmetic of a bank returning capital at roughly the pace it earns it. Book value per common share rose 7% to $39.34 and tangible book value per share 7% to $29.37 per the release.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow is the least useful of the three statements for a bank, and the vendor's table shows why: operating cash flow swings from -$8.8B in FY24 to $12.6B in FY25 and $45.0B in FY23 on trading and working-capital movements, capital expenditure is recorded as $0.00 because the template has no line for a bank's premises and technology spend, and the free cash flow row simply repeats operating cash flow. The trailing free cash flow yield of 22.4% is that artefact divided by market value, which is why no free-cash-flow or capital-expenditure cell appears in the snapshot; the two capital-return rows do, because they carry information.

Share repurchases rose to $24.1B in FY25 from $13.1B in FY24 and $4.6B in FY23, and dividends paid rose steadily from $8.1B in FY21 to $9.6B in FY25. The second quarter of 2026 continued the pattern, with the split between dividends and repurchases given under capital allocation, and on July 23, 2026 the Board raised the quarterly dividend to $0.32, an increase of 14 percent, payable September 25, 2026. Set beside the quarter's net income, the return rate is close to the full earnings of the period, which is sustainable only while CET1 stays comfortably above its minimum and risk-weighted asset growth stays moderate; the balance-sheet section carries those figures.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
At $59.47 the shares trade at 13.5x trailing earnings, 12.8x NTM earnings and ~11.3x FY27E EPS of $5.26, with a 1.95% dividend yield before the increase declared in July. The vendor's other multiples do not apply to a bank: EV/EBITDA of 24.7x capitalizes deposits as debt, and P/S of 2.2x divides by revenue gross of interest expense; peer multiples are pending a peer data source. The bank's own valuation anchors are the ones the release reports, book value per common share of $39.34 and tangible book value per share of $29.37, with return on average tangible common shareholders' equity of 17.0% in the quarter and 16.52% for the six months per the 10-Q.

The Street is constructive: 54 analysts, Buy 35, Hold 18, Sell 1, consensus Buy, with a consensus target of $66.00 (+11.0%), a median of $65.00 and a range of $59.00–$75.00. The shares sit in the upper part of their 52-week range of $46.12–$65.23. Our view is that a bank earning 17% on tangible equity and growing consensus EPS from $4.64 in FY26E toward the FY27E figure above deserves the forward multiple it has and a little more; the bull's argument is operating leverage, the bear's is that the numerator is at a cyclical peak in markets and investment banking and that a lower-rate path erodes net interest income.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Operating leverage holds in the 300-400 basis point range guided for 2026 and stays positive into 2027, net interest income keeps repricing higher while policy rates fall slowly, credit costs stay near the $1.4 billion quarterly run-rate, and the market pays a premium to the 12.8x NTM multiple for a 17% return on tangible equity; capital return continues at the second quarter's pace.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus is met: EPS of $4.64 in FY26E and $5.26 in FY27E, the CET1 ratio stays near 11.2% with repurchases absorbing the excess, and the shares hold roughly today's NTM multiple applied to FY27E earnings, which lands near the Street's $66.00 consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Policy rate cuts compress net interest income faster than fixed-rate repricing offsets, sales and trading and investment banking fall back from the quarter's 33% and 50% growth rates, provision rises as consumer and commercial credit normalize, and the multiple compresses toward the low end of the Street's $59.00–$75.00 target range and the 52-week low of $46.12.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 50% and split the remainder evenly between the Bull case at $80 and the Bear case at $50. The probability-weighted value lands on the consensus target quoted above, not by design, and sits at the bottom of the BUY envelope; our $62–$72 target range brackets the Base case at $67. The Base case is consensus delivered with a modest re-rating on the forward year, from the multiple the current price implies on FY27E to today's NTM multiple. The Bull case requires the operating-leverage guidance to hold into 2027 and the rate path to be gentle; we give it one chance in four because the six months to June already ran ahead of the guidance and the segment results were uniform, but the fee lines it depends on are the ones the risk section flags. The Bear case carries the same weight because the two things that produced the quarter, markets activity and repricing net interest income, are the two things a rate cycle can take away together.

A move to STRONG BUY would need the multiple, not the estimates, to be wrong, and we see no evidence for that while the fee cycle is at a high. A move to HOLD would follow a sales and trading decline or a rise in net charge-offs above the current run-rate, either of which would put the Bear case's mechanism in motion.

segments.name: Consumer Banking Segment
segments.body: Consumer Banking is the deposit engine. Second-quarter 2026 revenue was $11,336 million, up 5% on higher net interest income, and net income $3,281 million; provision fell to $1.2 billion with a reserve release of $23 million where a year earlier there was a build of $82 million, and the efficiency ratio was 51% with a 29% return on average allocated capital. Average deposits of $957 billion are up from pre-pandemic levels per the release, most of them in checking accounts, and the release ranks the bank first in U.S. consumer deposits on first-quarter 2026 FFIEC call-report data. The card book cuts the other way: the risk-adjusted margin slipped to 6.5% from 7.1% a year earlier as average balances grew to $103.6 billion.

segments.name: Global Wealth and Investment Management Segment
segments.body: GWIM is the segment with the most operating leverage. Second-quarter revenue rose 16% to $6,871 million on asset management fees up 19% to $4.4 billion, net income rose to $1,413 million from $993 million, and the pretax margin reached 27% from 22% a year earlier. Client balances were $4.9 trillion, up 12% mostly on market valuations, assets under management $2.3 trillion, up 17%, with AUM flows of $13.7 billion in the quarter and $78 billion since the second quarter of 2025; average loans grew 14% to $270 billion on custom and securities-based lending. Set against that, fee revenue moves with markets, and a quarter's flows are small beside the balance they are added to.

segments.name: Global Banking Segment
segments.body: Global Banking is the corporate lending, treasury and investment banking franchise. Second-quarter revenue rose 10% to $6.2 billion and net income 20% to more than $2 billion per the call, with total corporate investment banking fees excluding self-led deals up 50% to more than $2.1 billion across debt underwriting, advisory and equity underwriting. Average deposits rose 8% to $652 billion and average loans 7% to $413 billion, the release cites higher treasury service charges, and the return on average allocated capital was 15%. A jump of that size in fees is a market condition, not a share gain the pack can verify, and that is the caveat on the segment.

segments.name: Global Markets Segment
segments.body: Global Markets produced the quarter's sharpest growth. Sales and trading revenue was $7.1 billion including net DVA losses of $57 million, up 33% on either basis, with equities up 70% to $3.6 billion on client financing and derivatives and FICC up 9% to $3.5 billion; segment net income was $2.6 billion, and excluding DVA $2.7 billion. The release counts 17 consecutive quarters of year-over-year sales and trading growth and the call adds 14 consecutive quarters of net income growth, which shows a franchise that has held up across several market conditions; whether it has gained share the pack cannot say. This is also the segment most directly exposed to the market downturn the February 2026 10-K lists first among its risk factors, and its returns in the quarter were earned at the top of the activity cycle.

moatFactors.name: Deposit franchise
moatFactors.body: Average deposits stood at $2.02 trillion, the twelfth straight quarter of sequential growth per the release, and consumer deposits cost 48 basis points in the quarter per the call. Cheap, sticky funding is the moat of a universal bank, and it is why net interest income can rise year over year while policy rates fall. The margin available to absorb a rise in deposit costs is the net interest yield of 2.08 percent, the spread earned on average earning assets after funding cost; if deposit betas rise faster than asset yields reprice, that spread is where the damage shows.

moatFactors.name: Scale and digital distribution
moatFactors.body: The bank serves more than 69 million consumer and small business clients through approximately 3,500 financial centers, approximately 15,000 ATMs and approximately 50 million active digital users per the 10-Q; most consumer sales were digitally enabled in the quarter, 4.4 billion digital logins were counted, and 24.6 million clients used Erica. Scale shows in the efficiency ratio of 59% and the 6.6% of operating leverage. Scale also concentrates operational and regulatory exposure, which the 10-Q's list of open matters, from Zelle fraud to anti-money-laundering programs, illustrates.

moatFactors.name: Capital and balance sheet
moatFactors.body: CET1 capital of $202 billion and a CET1 ratio of 11.2% sit above the regulatory minimum management cites, average Global Liquidity Sources were $947 billion, and total assets of $3.5 trillion were funded by deposits of $2,025,124 million; the quarter's capital return left the ratio unchanged. The ceiling is regulatory rather than operational: stress capital buffers, total loss-absorbing capacity and the GSIB surcharge, all named in the 10-Q, decide how much can be returned, and they are not in the bank's hands.

moatFactors.name: Integrated model
moatFactors.body: Consumer Banking, GWIM and Global Banking feed each other: 38.7 million consumer checking accounts of which 92% are primary, $640 billion of consumer investment assets up 18% with $19 billion of net client flows, and approximately 6K net new $500K+ relationships across Merrill and the Private Bank in the quarter per the release. Integration cuts both ways: the wealth and markets businesses are the ones most sensitive to asset prices, so the model raises the beta of earnings to markets as well as the stickiness of clients.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is wide because the two things that make a universal bank durable, low-cost deposits and regulatory capital, are both in place and both growing, and because the four segments are each growing on their own account. What could erode it: a rate path that lifts deposit betas while asset yields fall, a credit cycle that the current $1.4 billion quarterly run-rate of net charge-offs does not anticipate, and a regulatory reset of capital rules. The consecutive-quarter streaks the release and the call count in deposits, loans and trading are evidence of a franchise that compounds through cycles; they are not evidence that the next quarter's fee revenue is sustainable, and we hold those two thoughts separately.

points: Management raised full-year operating leverage guidance to 300-400 basis points after the six months to June 2026 exceeded 450 basis points, up from the more than 200 basis points promised in April; at Investor Day the sustainable range was put at 200 to 300, so 2026 is running above the model, which also means 2027 starts from a high comparison base.

Net interest income is the growth engine: $16.0 billion in the quarter, up 9%, on fixed-rate asset repricing, loan growth and repayment of higher-cost funding, with net interest yield up to 2.08 percent; the six-month figure of $31,742 million compares with $29,113 million a year earlier. The counter is that repricing has to outrun the cutting cycle.

Loans are growing across every segment: average loans and leases of $1.22 trillion rose 8% for a ninth consecutive quarter of sequential growth, led by commercial loans up 11% to $733 billion. Growth concentrated in commercial lending at this point in the credit cycle is also where the next charge-offs would come from, and criticized commercial exposures, though falling, are still measured in the tens of billions.

Fee lines are growing faster than the balance sheet: noninterest income rose 22% with investment brokerage fees up 18% and asset management fees up 19% to $4.4 billion, and the two fee lines with the sharpest growth, investment banking and sales and trading, carry their figures in the moat and risk sections; the question the growth case must answer is how much of that repeats in a normal year.

Consensus has revenue of $124B in FY26E rising to $130.5B in FY27E, on the basis the financials section explains, and EPS of $4.64 rising to $5.26; the bank's own guidance is framed in operating leverage rather than earnings, and that guidance is consistent with the consensus path.

Client growth underneath: 160K+ net new consumer checking accounts for a thirtieth consecutive quarter of net growth, ~2 million BofA Rewards enrollments since the late-May relaunch, and approximately 6,000 net new affluent households in wealth; these are the inputs to next year's deposits and fees.

management.leadership: Brian T. Moynihan is Chair and CEO, as the July 14, 2026 release styles him, and the March 2026 proxy names Mr. Nowell as Lead Independent Director. The proxy sets out three independence requirements, the NYSE listing standards for a board majority and the audit, compensation and governance committees, the Federal Reserve's Enhanced Prudential Standards for the chair of the Enterprise Risk Committee, and the company's own Guidelines for a substantial majority, and it reports one determination: that every director and nominee other than Mr. Moynihan is independent. Alastair M. Borthwick is CFO. On execution the record is the quarter itself: every segment grew revenue and net income, every segment generated operating leverage, and the full-year guidance was raised mid-year rather than defended. Our reservation is about disclosure emphasis rather than conduct: the call and release lean on consecutive-quarter streaks and rankings, which are true as stated but say less about the next quarter than about the last several.
management.capitalAllocation: The framework is capital return sized to earnings under a regulatory ceiling. The bank returned $8.0 billion in the second quarter of 2026, $2.0 billion in common dividends and $6.0 billion in repurchases, so repurchases carry most of the payout and the 1.95% dividend yield understates it; the five-year repurchase and dividend series sits in the cash-flow section. The quarterly dividend goes to $0.32 from the $0.28 paid in the quarter, an increase of 14 percent. The constraint is the CET1 ratio of 11.2% and the rules behind it: capital returned at close to the pace of earnings holds the ratio flat only while risk-weighted assets grow slowly, and the 10-Q lists stress capital buffer requirements, total loss-absorbing capacity and the GSIB surcharge as variables the Board does not control. Our judgment is that the allocation is disciplined and the dividend increase is affordable; the risk is a regulatory change that resets the ceiling lower, not a management choice.
management.governance: The March 2026 proxy is the source. Say on Pay drew 73.6% of approximately 5.6 billion votes cast at the 2025 annual meeting. The proxy describes a year-round engagement practice: during 2025 the company reached out to 74 institutional shareholders representing approximately 67% of institutionally held shares and held 52 meetings with 31 of them. The proxy says the vote and that engagement informed the decision to keep the executive compensation design generally consistent; the tightening it describes, a higher performance standard for a 100% payout on the performance restricted stock units granted in February 2026 and the opportunity to earn up to 150% maximum payout, it attributes to the focus on long-term Responsible Growth discussed at the 2025 Investor Day. Our own reading is that a vote below three-quarters is the weakest signal in the proxy. Independence is documented director by director, with ordinary-course relationships tested at less than 2% of gross revenues, and the related-person policy routes transactions expected to exceed $120,000 in which a related person has a direct or indirect material interest to the Corporate Governance Committee, with stated exemptions. The proxy excerpt does not carry the pay tables, so we make no claim about pay levels.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy's ownership table as of March 13, 2026 shows that each director and named executive officer, and all directors and executive officers as a group of 25 persons, beneficially owned less than 1% of the common stock. Mr. Moynihan beneficially owned 2,803,195 shares with a further 1,724,434 unvested or cash-settled stock units, for 4,527,629 in total, and the group held 18,963,591 shares and units combined. Three holders sit above 5%: The Vanguard Group at 9.1%, Warren E. Buffett/Berkshire Hathaway Inc. at 7.9%, as the proxy names the filer, and BlackRock, Inc. at 6.9%. The two index managers vote a policy; that holder is a single concentrated voice large enough to be heard on capital return and succession, and the capital-return discipline this report credits to the Board is exercised with that holder present. Insider ownership is therefore economically meaningful to the executives but immaterial to control; the pack carries no insider transaction data.

idiosyncratic: Rate cycle and net interest income. The February 2026 10-K states that lower interest rates would typically result in lower revenue through lower net interest income, and notes that the Federal Reserve reduced policy rates in 2025 with the pace of further cuts uncertain. The offset management cites is fixed-rate asset repricing and the repayment of higher-cost funding, which lifted net interest yield to 2.08 percent; the risk is a cutting cycle fast enough that deposit rates lag while asset yields fall, or a curve that stays flat. Net interest income of $16.0 billion is the larger of the bank's two revenue lines, so a small move in yield is a large move in earnings.

Fee revenue at the top of the cycle. Sales and trading revenue of $7.1 billion, up 33%, and investment banking fees up 50% to $2.1 billion drove the quarter, and the release's own word for the markets quarter is exceptional; the 10-K's first-listed risk is a market downturn that reduces noninterest income. A return to the year-ago run-rate in these lines would remove much of the 15% revenue growth, and the equities line, up 70%, is the most exposed.

Credit normalization. Provision and net charge-offs of $1.4 billion each were flat to the March quarter and below a year earlier, and reservable criticized commercial exposures fell approximately $2.3 billion to roughly $22 billion, with non-performing loans at approximately $5.8 billion. The risk is the one the 10-Q names, credit losses higher than expected if unemployment, real estate prices or corporate spreads move, and the consumer card book's risk-adjusted margin already slipped to 6.5% from 7.1%. A modest reserve release in a quarter of loan growth means the allowance is not being built ahead of the cycle.

Litigation, regulation and operational exposure. The 10-Q's forward-looking statement lists open matters: unemployment-benefit processing for California and other states, the automatic credit card payment service, anti-money-laundering and sanctions programs, and Zelle-related fraud, with a possible change in how fraud losses are allocated between banks and customers. It also lists the capital rules, stress capital buffer, total loss-absorbing capacity and the GSIB surcharge. None is quantified in the pack, and the bank's own statement that liabilities may exceed its recorded liability and estimated range of loss is the risk in its own words.

Governance signal. Say on Pay support of 73.6% in 2025 is the lowest-conviction vote in the pack, and the Chair and CEO roles are combined in Mr. Moynihan, mitigated by a Lead Independent Director and an otherwise independent board; the proxy attributes its tightened equity-award standards to Investor Day and long-term Responsible Growth rather than to the vote. This is a watch item rather than a thesis risk.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposures are those of a global systemically important bank. The February 2026 10-K's market section runs from interest rates, inflation and Federal Reserve policy through fiscal and debt-ceiling risk, tariffs, geopolitical events, bank and nonbank failures and the volatility of digital assets; the 10-Q's forward-looking statement adds sovereign debt stress outside the U.S. and a deterioration in private credit markets. The bank's own research has 2026 U.S. GDP growth at 2.2% and global growth at 3.2% in 2026 and 3.5% in 2027, a benign base, and consumer spending was running at 6% plus year over year in the second quarter per the call. The mechanism to hold onto is that a downturn hits all three earnings lines at once, net interest income through rates, fees through markets and provision through credit, which is why the bear case is a real scenario rather than a formality.

body: **BUY, target range $62–$72.** The second quarter of 2026 showed a universal bank growing every segment, with every one of them adding operating leverage; the headline figures are revenue up 15%, diluted EPS of $1.21 and a 17.0% return on average tangible common equity, while CET1 stayed at 11.2% and the quarter's capital return ran close to the period's earnings. At 12.8x NTM earnings the shares trade below their trailing multiple, the operating-leverage guidance was raised mid-year, and the dividend was raised to $0.32.

What we are paying for is the deposit and lending franchise: deposits of $2.02 trillion on average, loans of $1.22 trillion growing 8%, and net interest income that rose 9% while policy rates fell. What we are wary of is the fee cycle and a rate path that can take net interest income the other way; the Bear case is what that looks like.

We would raise the target on operating leverage landing at the top of the 300-400 basis point range with credit costs flat, and we would move to HOLD on two consecutive quarters of sales and trading decline or on net charge-offs rising above the current run-rate. Our probability-weighted value sits at the consensus target, so the Street and we agree on the number; we differ only in reading the fee lines as the risk rather than the reward.
